extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factual rules for assessing novelty (anticipation, date of invention, burden of proof) and utility (ability to perform a good function) for patentability. Covers disclosure sufficiency (models/drawings/written descriptions), prior use/knowledge rules, forgotten-art limits, and utility doctrines for mechanical, compositional, and ornamental inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation independent of intended use of prior device
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation of novelty is not averted by the mere fact that the inventor of the prior device did not design it to perform the function of the patented device, nor by the mere fact that its ability to perform that function is not apparent to every beholder, nor by the mere fact that it was never actually used for that purpose, nor by any two of these facts combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same principle applies to a prior patent: although a prior patent may incidentally show a similar arrangement of parts, if that arrangement is not claimed nor designed to perform the function of the later patent, it cannot act as an anticipation. (Examples and authorities cited in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires the anticipating event to precede the inventor's date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is not negatived by anything which was invented, patented, or described in a printed publication prior to the granting of the patent sought to be anticipated, or even prior to the application therefor, unless the anticipating event occurred prior to the date of the invention secured by that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fixes that the relevant chronological cut-off is the date of the invention assignable to the patent, not merely the patent or publication date; the section discusses apparent exceptions and their resolution by looking to dates of invention. (Citations and case discussion provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority between two patents to the same inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two patents for the same invention are granted to the same inventor, the last, and not the first, is void, even where the last was first applied for; but the apparent exception is explained because both patents are entitled to date from the making of the invention and the first patent will negative the novelty of the last if the dates of invention are exactly the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains interplay with rule that first application usually represents first invention in absence of other evidence; identical inventor is evidence that invention dates may be identical. (Authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous generic vs specific applications rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When two applications by the same inventor are filed contemporaneously, one with generic claims and the other with specific claims, the inventor does not lose his right to the generic patent because it happens to issue after the issuance of the specific patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same rule applies where patentee files an improvement after filing for a generic invention and the improvement issues first; no express disclaimer of the first invention is necessary. (Cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent applications/patents that do not claim the same invention do not anticipate one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several applications describe the same structure or process, but no one of the issued patents claims any invention claimed in any of the others and they are all pending at the same time, the applications and patents cannot be used to anticipate each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule applies where none of the issued patents contains claims covering the others; explanation and authorities provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of invention fixed by sufficiently plain drawing, model, written description, or specimen
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the invention may be exhibited in a drawing or in a model, it will date from the completion of such a model or such a drawing as is sufficiently plain to enable those skilled in the art to understand the invention; where explained in words without model or drawing it will date from the completion of such a written description as would teach others how to make and use the invention; where a specimen was made it will date from completion of that specimen (substantial completeness enough).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patented inventions always date at least as early as the dates of the execution of the original applications therefor, provided the original applications exhibit the inventions with the mentioned sufficiency. Perfection is not necessary; substantial completeness suffices. (Cases: Loom Co. v. Higgins; National Cash Register Co. v. Store Service Co.; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental conception alone does not establish a date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: No invention ought to date from any day wherein it had no existence or representation outside of the mind of the inventor, no matter how clear or how complete his mental conception of its character and mode of operation may have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental conceptions are not useful inventions until embodied so the world could use them after the inventor's death; allowing mental conception to date inventions would tempt perjury. (Policy rationale provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral description can establish an earlier date if the hearer fully understood and remembered it
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an oral description given by the inventor to another of a subsequently patented invention can give that invention a date earlier than it would otherwise be entitled to depends on the nature of the invention and the capacity of the hearer to understand it and remember it; where the person understood it completely and remembered it accurately, a patented invention may date back to that oral description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstruse or complicated inventions where it's uncertain the hearer understood and remembered, the invention ought not to date from such a description. It is not necessary that all mechanical details be expressed in the disclosure. (Cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented incipiency dating vs unpatented incipiency disallowed for anticipations
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason for allowing a patented invention to date back to an oral/written description or drawing/model, while an unpatented invention set up to negative the novelty of a patent is not allowed to date back to such incipiency, is that patents are ultimate developments and ought equitably to date from such incipiency, while the rights of a patentee ought not be impaired by a similar incipiency never developed into a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains equitable distinction between developed (patented) disclosures and mere incipient, undeveloped disclosures asserted as anticipations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of the anticipating event is immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is questioned in point of novelty depending upon the date of the invention claimed, it is not material whether the event which constituted that invention occurred in the United States or in some other country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short statement; references an extended discussion of priority of date between inventors in cited case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior knowledge and use in the country negates novelty even if secret or by a single person
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is negatived by prior knowledge and use in this country, by even a single person, of the thing patented; this rule applies even to cases where that knowledge and use were purposely kept secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule applies irrespective of whether the prior structure was used; cases cited (e.g., Coffin v. Ogden and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgotten-art doctrine limited to processes and does not apply to machines, manufactures, compositions, or designs that can be found
rubrics_metrics.description: A single instance of prior knowledge and use will not negative novelty if that use had ceased and that knowledge was forgotten until called to mind by reinvention (Gayler v. Wilder), but this doctrine applies to a forgotten 'art' or 'process' (intangible) and is not applicable to a machine, manufacture, composition of matter or design which still exists and can be found or identified by diligent search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains limits: forgotten process may not anticipate; tangible items that can be located or analyzed do anticipate; examples given (use of gypsum between safe walls in Gayler v. Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a prior specimen in country can negate novelty but identity must be knowable
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is negatived by evidence that even one specimen of the thing patented existed and was known in this country prior to its invention by the patentee, even though it was not used prior to that time; however, if the identity of the patented and prior article can be known only by actual use and the prior article was not actually used until after the patent date, then its prior existence will not negative novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge to negative novelty must include knowledge of the character as well as the existence of the prior thing. (Authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's ignorance of anticipating matter does not avert negation of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation of novelty is not averted by the fact that the inventor had no knowledge of the anticipating matter when he made the invention covered by the patent; patent laws do not reward people for producing things new to them but old to others in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct statement; cases cited (e.g., Derby v. Thompson; Many v. Sizer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different material, process, or source does not avoid anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation of novelty in a machine is not averted by the fact that the anticipating machine operated upon a different material. And negation of novelty in a manufacture or a composition of matter is not averted by the fact that the anticipating substance was made by a different process or derived from a different source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It does not make an old thing new to derive it from a new quarter or to make it by a new method. (Cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions of novelty are questions of fact (not mere construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of novelty are questions of fact; even where the prior thing is a patent or printed publication and terms might require construction, the question whether the novelty of a patent is negatived by a prior patent depends upon the outward embodiment of terms in the prior document and is properly sought and explained by evidence in pais; such questions belong to evidence, not construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court treats such matters as factual inquiries; supporting authorities and illustrations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and degree of proof required to establish lack of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof of a want of novelty rests upon him who avers it, and every reasonable doubt should be resolved against him. Novelty can only be negatived by proof which puts the fact beyond a reasonable doubt, though various formulations of required proof (full, unequivocal and convincing; clear and satisfactory; strong and convincing) have been used and the exact degree is stated in many ways in the authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise lists many case-formulations (e.g., 'beyond a reasonable doubt'; 'clear and convincing'; 'strong and convincing') and notes that applying the 'reasonable doubt' phrase as in criminal law has few parallels in civil jurisprudence; examples and citations given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting burden when anticipation proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an anticipating fact prior to the date of a patent is proved beyond reasonable doubt, the burden is shifted to the plaintiff to prove, by convincing preponderance of evidence, that his invention was made still earlier than that fact occurred; failure to introduce enough evidence to strongly outweigh contrary evidence renders patent void for want of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains practical effect of successfully proven anticipation and the degree of evidence needed to rebut it; authorities cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception in Ninth Circuit re: pending application for same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception to the 'reasonable doubt' rule has been noted in the Ninth Circuit where the question of priority is at issue and at the time of issuance of the patent in suit the defendant had an application pending for the same invention and no interference was declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted as a circuit-specific treatment; citation indicated in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility: requirement that a thing or process produce a good result
rubrics_metrics.description: To possess utility, a thing or a process must be capable of producing a result, and that result must be a good result. Both elements inhere in the meaning of the word and require separate explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text frames utility as statutory requirement to promote the useful arts; references to Revised Statutes and statutory history provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility, although it may have had meaning for design patents in earlier law, is not required under the present law as an element of a design patent; a design that consists merely of a new and ornamental shape is still patentable as such and need not be made for sole purpose of ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References statutory provisions and amendments (e.g., Revised Statutes sections) and cases discussing design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperable devices lack utility (utility negatived by lack of function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is absent from all processes and devices which cannot be used to perform their specified functions, and patents for such subjects are therefore void. The patent is void if the machine will not answer the purpose for which it was intended without some addition, adjustment, or alteration which the mechanic must introduce of his own invention not invented by the patentee at the time of issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: Burrall v. Jewett (threshing-cylinder which was useless), Bliss v. Brooklyn (hose-coupling inoperative until lug added); judge holdings described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection not necessary to utility; imperfect performance suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention performs a good function, though imperfectly, its utility is not negatived by the fact that it is susceptible of improvement which will make it operate much better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility is not vitiated merely because prior inventions performed the same function as well or better, or by later superior inventions that entirely supersede the patented thing; patents are not void merely because the thing performs poorly—public harm from exclusivity may be minimal. (Cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility in ornamental manufactures: beauty is utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility in a manufacture is not negatived by the fact that it has no function except to decorate the object to which it is designed to be attached. In such cases utility resides in beauty—whatever is beautiful is useful because beauty gives pleasure, and pleasure is a kind of happiness, and happiness is a kind of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that ornamental designs may satisfy utility requirement for manufactures; statutory and case support referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility negated where function is evil; doubts resolved against infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is negatived by lack of function and is also negatived where the function is evil; doubts relevant to utility should be solved against infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text summarizes policy stance that functions considered immoral or harmful defeat utility; instructs courts to resolve doubtful utility questions against those asserting infringement.
